name: Uhl anomaly
aliases: congenital absence of right ventricular myocardium

reference.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease / congenital cardiomyopathy literature
clinicalPearls: A rare congenital disorder marked by near-total absence of the right ventricular myocardium
The right ventricular free wall is reduced to apposed layers of endocardium and epicardium, giving a paper-thin parchment appearance
Presents with right heart failure, often in infancy or childhood, and can cause arrhythmia and sudden death
The thin-walled right ventricle dilates and fails to contract, producing markedly impaired right ventricular function
Must be distinguished from arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, in which myocardium is replaced by fibrofatty tissue
Imaging shows an aneurysmal, akinetic, extremely thin right ventricular free wall with preserved left ventricle early on
Management is supportive for heart failure and arrhythmia, with transplantation considered in end-stage disease
reference.pathophysiology: Uhl anomaly is a congenital cardiomyopathy in which the right ventricular myocardium is almost entirely absent, so the free wall consists of directly apposed endocardium and epicardium with little or no intervening muscle. This is thought to arise from an excessive developmental loss of right ventricular myocytes, in contrast to the progressive fibrofatty myocardial replacement of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. The resulting parchment-thin wall cannot generate contractile force, leading to a dilated, akinetic right ventricle, progressive right heart failure, and a substrate for ventricular arrhythmia.
additionalDifferentials: Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
Idiopathic dilatation of the right atrium and ventricle
Severe pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular failure
Congenital tricuspid regurgitation from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography demonstrating a dilated, thin-walled, akinetic right ventricle
Cardiac MRI to characterise wall thinning and distinguish it from fibrofatty replacement
ECG and ambulatory monitoring to detect right-sided conduction and arrhythmia
Assessment of right ventricular function and heart-failure severity
Family and genetic evaluation to help separate it from arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
redFlags: Progressive right heart failure in infancy or childhood
Signs suggesting risk of sudden cardiac death
Severe right ventricular dilatation with haemodynamic compromise
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally poor, with many patients developing progressive right heart failure and arrhythmia; survival varies with severity, and advanced disease may ultimately require cardiac transplantation.
pitfalls: Confusing it with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, which has different genetics and management
Overlooking the arrhythmic and sudden-death risk while focusing on heart failure
Misattributing right heart failure to pulmonary or valvular causes
Underestimating disease severity from a preserved left ventricle early in the course
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
